n: With the land divided, the Lord gives Joshua instructions to set up a justice system. Settling the land includes protecting human life.

f.w: The LORD also spake unto Joshua

n: The Lord reminds Israel of the cities of refuge He had already commanded through Moses. Now it is time to name them.

f.g: Through Moses as the Lord’s messenger.

n: A person who killed someone by accident could flee to a refuge city for protection from the victim’s relative seeking revenge. God’s law distinguished accident from murder.

f.g: Hebrew go’el, the nearest kinsman, responsible for avenging a family member’s death.

n: The fugitive explains his case to the elders at the city gate, the usual place of judgment. If they accept it, they take him in and give him a place to live.

f.g: City gates were where elders met to hear cases.

n: The city must not hand him over to the avenger, because the death was not planned and came from no prior hatred.

f.g: Had no earlier hostility toward him.

n: He stays until his case is formally judged and until the high priest dies; then he may go home in safety. Many see in this a picture of how the death of a High Priest — Christ — sets the guilty free.

f.w: until the death of the high priest

f.g: Face a formal hearing by the community.

n: Three refuge cities are named west of the Jordan — north, center, and south — so that no one was ever too far from safety.
Three more refuge cities lie east of the Jordan, which Moses had already chosen.
The cities protected both Israelites and foreigners living among them. God’s mercy and fair hearing extended to the stranger too.

f.g: A foreign resident living among Israel.
